question.text: Which of the following is TRUE about market bubbles as discussed in the workbook's bubble section, drawing on Keith Redhead (2008)?

answer.text: Bubbles only form in equity markets and never in commodity or real estate markets
Sir Isaac Newton profited from the Dutch Tulip Mania of the 1630s by selling early
Conditions that foster bubbles include a high proportion of inexperienced traders, high uncertainty about true value, possible borrowing-financed purchases, and difficulty in short selling
Tulip Mania was a minor historical episode and not associated with bubble conditions in the workbook

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook's bubble section, citing Keith Redhead (2008), lists the conditions under which bubbles tend to emerge: a high proportion of inexperienced traders in the market, high uncertainty about the true value of the asset, the possibility of purchases financed by borrowing, and difficulty in short selling. The chapter discusses these alongside Kindleberger's framing of bubbles and crashes. The Trap: The Newton-Tulip story option is incorrect. Saying tulip-era episodes are absent from the workbook's bubble discussion is wrong, and restricting bubbles to equities ignores the multiple asset-class examples used. Note: Attribute the four listed bubble-emergence conditions to Keith Redhead (2008) as the workbook does, even when the broader section also references Kindleberger.
